name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Thursday 11 January 1973

clue.text: Springs after Miss Liddell in Australia

definitions.text: Springs after Miss Liddell in Australia

blocks.note: surface reading: some springs, or leaps, made after a young lady called Liddell
setter's reading: the Australian town whose name is completed by the word Springs, which is also the first name of Lewis Carroll's muse Miss Liddell

explanation.surface: Someone goes bounding after a Miss Liddell somewhere in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: Alice Liddell was the girl for whom Lewis Carroll wrote Alice in Wonderland; Alice Springs is a town in the Northern Territory.
explanation.definitionFit: The name serves twice: Carroll's young friend was called this, and the outback town takes it before the word Springs.

clue.text: Plenty of solo achievement

blocks.note: first meaning: a great quantity
second meaning: in the card game solo whist, a bid to take nine tricks

explanation.surface: Someone has done very well working alone.
explanation.walkthrough: Solo whist is a card game in which one player bids against the other three; its bids include misère and this one.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a copious supply, and it is also the named bid in solo whist promising nine tricks.

clue.text: Finger of power?

blocks.note: first meaning: the forefinger, next to the thumb
second meaning: in mathematics, the exponent to which a number is raised

explanation.surface: A finger that wields authority, perhaps a pointing one.
explanation.definitionFit: The forefinger carries this name, and mathematicians use the same word for an exponent written above a number.

clue.text: Matabele men talk with spirit evidently

definitions.note: the answer is used here as a noun, a nature spirit

indicators.note: what is evident is plainly visible, so the answer can be seen sitting openly in the clue's letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of Matabele, all of men and the start of talk

explanation.surface: Men of the Matabele people speak with great spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: The Matabele (Ndebele) are a people of Zimbabwe.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun this word names a supernatural being tied to one of the classical elements, a kind of spirit.

clue.text: He thought, therefore, he was a philosopher

definitions.text: He thought, therefore, he was a philosopher

blocks.clueFragment: He thought, therefore, he was a philosopher
blocks.note: surface reading: someone concluded from his own reasoning that he was a philosopher
setter's reading: a twist on the famous Latin maxim 'I think, therefore I am', so the man is its French author

explanation.surface: A man reasons his way to the conclusion that he must be a philosopher.
explanation.definitionFit: The seventeenth-century French thinker wrote cogito ergo sum, which the clue recasts in the past tense.

clue.text: Slip out during the day for a show

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or out of place, so these letters are rearranged
something happening during a period sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Sneaking away in the daytime to catch a performance.
explanation.definitionFit: A show or exhibition is something set out for people to look at, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Team transport?

blocks.note: surface reading: a coach or bus carrying a sports team
setter's reading: the team is a motorcycle racing pair, rider and passenger, who travel in a motorbike with an attached car

explanation.walkthrough: Sidecar racing uses two-person crews, so the attached passenger pod is literally team transport.
explanation.definitionFit: This one-wheeled passenger compartment bolted to a motorcycle carries a crew of two, the rider and a passenger.

clue.text: Prize for Cricket on the Hearth

blocks.note: first meaning: the urn contested by England and Australia in Test cricket
second meaning: the burnt remains of a fire lying in the fireplace

explanation.surface: An award for Dickens's story The Cricket on the Hearth.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cricket on the Hearth is a Dickens Christmas book; splitting it after Cricket reveals the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: The trophy series between England and Australia is named after a tiny urn, and the same word is the residue left in a grate.

clue.text: Tory trier thrown out of ground

indicators.note: things thrown out land scattered in disarray, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of both words taken together

explanation.surface: A Conservative who keeps trying gets ejected from the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Land or ground under someone's control, or an area of land in general, is a synonym for this word.

clue.text: Break up a strong effort to make a point in court

definitions.text: a strong effort to make a point in court

blocks.note: first meaning: to shatter into pieces

blocks.clueFragment: a strong effort to make a point in court
blocks.note: second meaning: in tennis, a hard overhead shot hit down to win the point

explanation.surface: A lawyer's forceful argument in a courtroom breaks up the proceedings.
explanation.walkthrough: The court is a tennis court, not a law court.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means shatter violently; as a noun it is the powerful downward tennis stroke meant to win a rally.

clue.text: Like raw hide — or showing it

blocks.note: first meaning: of leather, not yet treated or finished
second meaning: hide read as one's own skin, so wearing no clothes

explanation.surface: Something like untanned leather, or exposing it.
explanation.definitionFit: Untreated skins are described this way by tanners, and a naked person is also described with the same word.

clue.text: He came to Britain — his brother gave the sign

definitions.text: He came to Britain — his brother gave the sign

blocks.note: surface reading: some immigrant whose brother gestured
setter's reading: the brother is Hengist, the Saxon leader who in legend gave the signal for the massacre of the Britons at a feast

explanation.surface: A man arrives in Britain after his brother signals to him.
explanation.walkthrough: Hengist and his brother led the Anglo-Saxon arrival in Kent in the fifth century, according to legend.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary Jutish chieftain arrived in Kent with his brother Hengist around 449 AD.

clue.text: Land of Pot?

blocks.note: first meaning: a name for the southern states of the USA
second meaning: a large metal cooking pot used by soldiers

explanation.surface: A country called Pot, or perhaps a place where cannabis grows.
explanation.walkthrough: A dixie is British army slang for a camp kettle or mess tin.
explanation.definitionFit: The American South is nicknamed this, and soldiers call their big iron cooking kettle by the same word.

clue.text: Craftsman in a key industry

blocks.note: surface reading: an industry vital to the economy
setter's reading: key taken literally, so a craftsman whose trade is making keys and locks

explanation.surface: A skilled worker employed in one of the nation's vital industries.
explanation.definitionFit: This tradesman makes and repairs locks and cuts keys, so his industry is literally one of keys.

clue.text: " she sings on yon pomegranate tree:" (R and )

definitions.text: " she sings on yon pomegranate tree:"

blocks.clueFragment: " she sings on yon pomegranate tree:"
blocks.note: surface reading: a line of verse with its opening word missing
setter's reading: the source is Romeo and Juliet, where Juliet says the nightingale sings there each night; the missing word fills the gap

explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue lost the answer from the quotation and the J from the source; Juliet's line in Act 3 begins with the missing adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: Juliet tells Romeo the bird sings on the pomegranate every night, so the adverb meaning each night completes the line.

clue.text: While the apes stay, there stay we

definitions.text: While the apes stay, there stay we

blocks.note: surface reading: a vow to remain as long as some monkeys do
setter's reading: the legend that Britain will hold its Mediterranean rock as long as the Barbary macaques live there

explanation.surface: A solemn pledge to remain wherever the monkeys remain.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend holds British rule over the rock at the mouth of the Mediterranean lasts while its Barbary macaques survive.

clue.text: Soldier fitted to be with the Colours

blocks.clueFragment: fitted to be with the Colours
blocks.note: surface reading: someone fit to serve under the regimental flags
setter's reading: fitted means dressed, in a scarlet tunic, the colour of old British infantry

explanation.surface: A soldier judged fit to serve with the regimental flags.
explanation.walkthrough: With the Colours means serving in the army; the colour that matters is the scarlet of the tunic.
explanation.definitionFit: British soldiers of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries were nicknamed for their scarlet tunics.

clue.text: The stage-coach industry

blocks.note: first meaning: a French or continental public stagecoach
second meaning: steady hard work

explanation.surface: The business of running stagecoaches.
explanation.definitionFit: Industry in the sense of hard-working application is a synonym, and the same word named the old French public coach.

clue.text: Cuddly Theodore, honey lover

definitions.note: an adjective here, while the answer is a noun, a cuddly toy

blocks.note: a familiar short form of the name
an animal famous for raiding hives

explanation.surface: A huggable man named Theodore who loves honey.
explanation.walkthrough: The toy is named after Theodore Roosevelt, so the wordplay doubles as its history.
explanation.definitionFit: The stuffed toy animal children hug at bedtime is the classic cuddly thing.

clue.text: Preserves oriental doctor with charity

blocks.note: E for eastern
Bachelor of Medicine, a medical degree
gifts given to the poor

explanation.surface: An Eastern physician keeps things with charitable gifts.
explanation.definitionFit: Preserving a corpse from decay with chemicals is exactly what this verb describes.

clue.text: Shout as street carollers do

blocks.note: first meaning: to call out loudly
second meaning: carol singers perform aloud in the open

explanation.surface: Bellowing the way carol singers in the street do.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means call out loudly, and literally describes singing loudly outdoors at Christmas.

clue.text: Secured by jack with a pin

blocks.note: surface reading: fastened by someone called Jack using a pin
setter's reading: jack is a sailor, who makes ropes fast around a wooden pin on a ship's rail

explanation.surface: Something fastened by Jack with a pin.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack, or jack tar, is a sailor; sailors fasten ropes with a belaying pin.
explanation.definitionFit: The nautical verb means to make a rope fast around a cleat or pin, so it means secured.

clue.text: Born a Shylock but a good mixer "

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for born
Shakespeare's Shylock is a moneylender

explanation.surface: Someone born a miser, yet sociable.
explanation.walkthrough: Shylock is the moneylender in The Merchant of Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen appliance that whirls ingredients together is a machine designed to mix food well.

clue.text: Dare to tail Conan Doyle's professor

indicators.note: to tail something is to cut off its tail, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: Professor Challenger, hero of The Lost World

explanation.surface: Daring someone to follow the professor in Conan Doyle's stories.
explanation.walkthrough: To tail looks like follow; here it means remove the tail.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb and noun it means to dare or defy someone to do something.

clue.text: Paper cap

blocks.note: first meaning: a traditional size of printing paper
second meaning: an artificial covering fitted over a tooth

explanation.surface: A hat made of paper, as found in a Christmas cracker.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard old sheet size of paper carries this name, and dentists fit the same thing over a damaged tooth.

clue.text: Where only an uncouth churl would leave a lady

definitions.text: Where only an uncouth churl would leave a lady

indicators.note: uncouth means rough and unpolished, so the following word is roughed up into a new order

blocks.note: a churl is a rude, boorish man

explanation.surface: Only a boor would abandon a woman like this.
explanation.walkthrough: To leave someone in the lurch is to desert them in difficulty; the whole clue describes that spot.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom leave in the lurch means to abandon someone when they need help, the place a rude man would desert her.

clue.text: "Time you old man Will you not stay?" (Hodgson)

definitions.text: "Time you old man Will you not stay?"

blocks.clueFragment: "Time you old man Will you not stay?"
blocks.note: surface reading: a line of verse with a word missing after old
setter's reading: Ralph Hodgson's poem 'Time

explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue lost the answer from the quotation; Hodgson's poem asks Time, a wandering traveller, to halt.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Ralph Hodgson's 1917 poem addresses Time as a wandering traveller, filling the gap after old.

clue.text: Sock puppet?

blocks.note: first meaning: a hard blow with the fist
second meaning: the hook-nosed hero of the traditional ... and Judy show

explanation.surface: A puppet made from a sock.
explanation.walkthrough: Sock is slang for a hit, not a stocking.
explanation.definitionFit: A thump with the fist is a synonym, and the same name belongs to the glove puppet who quarrels with Judy.

clue.text: Set route to be on target

definitions.note: a phrase for a hit on the target, while the answer is a noun naming that hit

indicators.note: to set something is to arrange it, so the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Planning a course so as to stay on track.
explanation.definitionFit: In archery or shooting, the outermost ring of the target, or a shot landing there, is still a hit.

clue.text: In entering the Gold Ball observe the regulation

indicators.note: a word entering another goes inside it

blocks.note: or is gold in heraldry
a ball is a formal dance
taken as written

explanation.surface: Follow the rules on coming into the Gold Ball.
explanation.definitionFit: A decree or bylaw issued by an authority is a regulation, a direct synonym.

clue.text: One may find pointers to it in The Plough

definitions.text: One may find pointers to it in The Plough

blocks.clueFragment: pointers to it in The Plough
blocks.note: surface reading: clues or tips found in a pub called The Plough, or a farm implement
setter's reading: the constellation also called the Big Dipper, whose two Pointer stars line up with the pole star

explanation.surface: Hints towards something might be picked up in a pub called The Plough.
explanation.walkthrough: The Plough is the British name for the Big Dipper.
explanation.definitionFit: Polaris, the pole star, is located by extending the line through the two Pointer stars of the Plough.

clue.text: It's a knock-out or thereabouts

indicators.note: abouts suggests turning about, so the preceding letters are turned into a fresh order

blocks.note: the first five letters of this word are the fodder; the rest is the signal

explanation.surface: Something is a stunning success, or near enough.
explanation.walkthrough: Thereabouts splits into the fodder and its signal.
explanation.definitionFit: This volatile liquid was the classic anaesthetic, used to render patients unconscious before surgery.
